blocks.text: A steel test bar stretches evenly, then a waist suddenly forms in the middle of the gauge length and the load on the testing machine starts to fall, even though the metal in the neck is getting stronger. The two ways of defining stress and strain explain this apparent paradox.

blocks.markdown: The tensile test pulls a standard specimen at a constant rate while recording load $F$ and extension $\Delta l$. Dividing by the original area $A_0$ and original length $l_0$ gives **engineering** quantities, which depend only on the starting geometry and are convenient for design. Dividing by the instantaneous area and length gives **true** quantities, which describe what the metal itself experiences.

blocks.title: Engineering and true stress and strain
blocks.text: Engineering stress $\sigma=F/A_0$ (Pa) and engineering strain $\varepsilon=\Delta l/l_0$ (dimensionless). True stress $\sigma_T=F/A$, where $A$ is the instantaneous cross-sectional area, and true strain $\varepsilon_T=\int \mathrm{d}l/l=\ln(l/l_0)$.

blocks.caption: Valid below necking, where deformation is uniform and volume is constant ($A\,l=A_0\,l_0$).

blocks.title: Reading the 0.2 percent offset yield strength
blocks.prompt: A metal has initial slope $E=200$ GPa (the curve passes 300 MPa at strain 0.0015). Curve data beyond the elastic limit are: strain 0.0030 at 330 MPa, strain 0.0040 at 345 MPa. Find the 0.2 percent offset yield strength.

steps.text: The offset line has the elastic slope and starts at strain 0.002: $\sigma_{off}=E(\varepsilon-0.002)$.
At $\varepsilon=0.0030$: line $=200$ MPa, curve $=330$ MPa (curve above the line). At $\varepsilon=0.0040$: line $=400$ MPa, curve $=345$ MPa (curve below).
Interpolate the crossing: fraction $=130/(130+55)=0.703$, so $\varepsilon=0.0030+0.703(0.0010)=0.0037$ and $\sigma=330+0.703(15)\approx340.5$ MPa.

blocks.answer: The 0.2 percent offset yield strength is about 340 MPa, found where the offset line crosses the curve.

blocks.markdown: **Key points on the curve.** The *yield strength* $\sigma_y$ marks the start of permanent deformation (taken with the 0.2 percent offset if no sharp yield point). The *ultimate tensile strength* (UTS) is the maximum engineering stress, $F_{max}/A_0$. *Ductility* is the plastic deformation at fracture, expressed as percentage elongation $100(l_f-l_0)/l_0$ or percentage reduction in area $100(A_0-A_f)/A_0$.

rows: Measured at the neck after fracture
blocks.caption: Properties read from an engineering stress-strain curve.

blocks.title: Converting engineering values to true values
blocks.prompt: A specimen is loaded to an engineering stress of 300 MPa at an engineering strain of 0.12, before necking. Find the true stress and the true strain.

steps.text: Check that deformation is uniform: this point is below the UTS, so the conversion formulas apply.

blocks.answer: $\sigma_T=336$ MPa and $\varepsilon_T=0.113$; the true values differ from the engineering values by about 12 percent in stress and 6 percent in strain.

blocks.markdown: **Necking.** Plastic deformation hardens the metal, which raises $\sigma_T$, but it also reduces the area, which lowers the load capacity of the cross-section. The load is $F=\sigma_T A$. Early on, hardening wins and $F$ rises. At the point of maximum load the two effects are equal, $\mathrm{d}F=0$, and any small local thinning becomes unstable: a neck forms. Afterwards the area at the neck falls faster than the metal hardens, the load drops, and the engineering stress $F/A_0$ falls. The true stress $F/A$ at the neck keeps rising because the metal in the neck is still hardening.

items: The UTS is at maximum load, where necking begins; it is not the fracture stress.
The true stress-strain curve is monotonic; the engineering curve has a maximum.
Conversion formulas $\sigma_T=\sigma(1+\varepsilon)$ and $\varepsilon_T=\ln(1+\varepsilon)$ hold only before necking.
After necking, the true stress needs the measured neck area, not the specimen length.

blocks.title: Conversion limits
blocks.text: The formulas rely on uniform deformation. Applying them past the UTS gives wrong values because the strain is concentrated in the neck and the gauge-length strain does not represent it.

points: Yield strength (0.2 percent offset), UTS ($F_{max}/A_0$) and ductility (elongation, reduction in area) are the key quantities read from an engineering curve.
The engineering curve falls after necking because it uses the original area, while the true curve keeps rising as the metal strain hardens.

questions.stem: Many metals have no sharp yield point, so yield strength is usually defined by the 0.2 percent offset method. What does this method do?

options.text: It draws a line parallel to the elastic slope, starting at 0.002 strain, and takes the stress where it meets the curve
It takes the stress at 0.2 percent total strain
It takes 0.2 times the ultimate tensile strength
It takes the stress at which the specimen first necks

questions.correctOptionText: It draws a line parallel to the elastic slope, starting at 0.002 strain, and takes the stress where it meets the curve

distractorRationale.a: Correct: this is the stress that leaves 0.2 percent permanent strain on unloading.
distractorRationale.b: This ignores the offset; at 0.2 percent total strain the elastic strain is included and the plastic strain is smaller.
distractorRationale.c: This is not a definition; the proof stress comes from the curve, not from a fraction of the UTS.
distractorRationale.d: Necking occurs at the maximum load and is a different point on the curve.

questions.explanation: With no clear knee in the curve, a construction line of slope $E$ is offset by a plastic strain of 0.002 and the intersection with the curve is the proof or yield stress. Unloading from that point along a line parallel to the elastic slope leaves 0.2 percent permanent strain.

questions.stem: On an engineering stress-strain curve, what is the ultimate tensile strength (UTS)?

options.text: The maximum engineering stress reached, which is the maximum load divided by the original cross-sectional area
The engineering stress at which the specimen fractures
The stress at which plastic deformation begins
The maximum true stress, which occurs at fracture

questions.correctOptionText: The maximum engineering stress reached, which is the maximum load divided by the original cross-sectional area

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the peak of the engineering curve.
distractorRationale.b: Fracture stress is generally lower than the UTS for ductile metals, because the curve falls after necking.
distractorRationale.d: The true stress is highest at fracture, but the UTS is defined on the engineering curve.

questions.explanation: The UTS is the peak of the engineering curve, $F_{max}/A_0$. For a ductile metal it is reached at the onset of necking and is always greater than or equal to the yield strength.

questions.stem: For a specimen in uniform tension below necking, the true stress is greater than the engineering stress.
questions.explanation: Below necking $\sigma_T=\sigma(1+\varepsilon)$, and since $\varepsilon>0$ in tension, $\sigma_T>\sigma$. The reason is that the cross-sectional area decreases as the specimen lengthens, while the engineering stress uses the original area.

questions.stem: A cylindrical tensile specimen of original diameter 10.0 mm fractures with a minimum diameter of 6.4 mm at the neck. Calculate the percentage reduction in area, a measure of ductility.
questions.explanation: Percentage reduction in area is $100(A_0-A_f)/A_0=100\,[1-(d_f/d_0)^2]$. With $d_f/d_0=0.64$, $(0.64)^2=0.4096$, so the reduction is $100\times0.5904=59.0$ percent.

questions.stem: A metal is pulled uniformly (before any necking) to an engineering strain of 0.08 under an engineering stress of 450 MPa. Calculate the true stress in MPa.
questions.explanation: Assuming constant volume and uniform deformation, $\sigma_T=\sigma(1+\varepsilon)=450\times1.08=486$ MPa. The true stress is higher because the cross-section has shrunk.

questions.stem: A test, analysed below necking, records a true stress of 700 MPa at a true strain of 0.15. Calculate the corresponding engineering stress in MPa.
questions.explanation: True strain gives engineering strain: $\varepsilon=e^{\varepsilon_T}-1=e^{0.15}-1=0.1618$. Then $\sigma=\sigma_T/(1+\varepsilon)=700/1.1618=602.5$ MPa.

questions.stem: At what point on the engineering stress-strain curve of a ductile metal does necking begin?

options.text: At the maximum load, the UTS
At the 0.2 percent offset yield point

questions.correctOptionText: At the maximum load, the UTS

distractorRationale.a: Correct: beyond this point strain hardening can no longer offset the loss of area and deformation localises.
distractorRationale.b: Yielding is followed by uniform plastic deformation, with no neck yet.
distractorRationale.c: Fracture ends the test after the neck has grown; necking begins much earlier.
distractorRationale.d: The proportional limit is in the elastic range, far from necking.

questions.explanation: Necking starts at maximum load, where the increase in flow stress from strain hardening is exactly balanced by the decrease in cross-sectional area (the Considere condition $\mathrm{d}\sigma_T/\mathrm{d}\varepsilon_T=\sigma_T$). After that the deformation concentrates in the neck.

questions.stem: After necking, the engineering stress-strain curve falls while the true stress-strain curve continues to rise. What is the correct explanation?

options.text: Engineering stress divides the load by the original area, but the neck's area shrinks so fast that the load falls; the true stress uses the actual smaller area and keeps rising as the metal strain hardens
The metal softens after necking, so true stress also decreases
The true stress curve is wrong after necking because the volume is not constant
The load increases after necking, but the extensometer is wrong

questions.correctOptionText: Engineering stress divides the load by the original area, but the neck's area shrinks so fast that the load falls; the true stress uses the actual smaller area and keeps rising as the metal strain hardens

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the metal is still hardening, but the engineering stress ignores the area loss.
distractorRationale.b: The true stress, found with the actual neck area, continues to rise because strain hardening continues.
distractorRationale.c: Volume is roughly conserved; the practical problem is that the strain in the neck is non-uniform, not that the curve is physically wrong.
distractorRationale.d: The load actually decreases after the UTS; the instrument is not at fault.

questions.explanation: The load $F=\sigma_T A$ falls after necking because $A$ at the neck decreases faster than $\sigma_T$ increases. The engineering stress is $F/A_0$, so it falls with the load, but the true stress $F/A$ keeps rising because the metal strain hardens.

questions.stem: Explain why the engineering stress-strain curve of a ductile metal reaches a maximum and then falls before fracture, whereas the true stress-strain curve continues to rise. Refer to the load, the cross-sectional area and strain hardening.
markingGuide: Engineering stress $=F/A_0$ with fixed original area (1 mark)
True stress $=F/A$ with the instantaneous area (1 mark)
Strain hardening increases flow stress as strain increases (1 mark)
Early in the test, hardening outpaces the loss of area, so the load rises (1 mark)
At the UTS the two effects balance: $\mathrm{d}F=0$ (1 mark), and necking begins, localising the strain
After necking the area loss at the neck dominates, so the load and engineering stress fall (1 mark)
The true stress continues to rise because the metal keeps hardening (1 mark)
questions.explanation: Load is the product of true stress and area, so it rises while hardening wins and falls when the shrinking neck wins. Engineering stress follows the load, while true stress follows the hardening of the material itself.

questions.stem: A tensile test on a 10.0 mm diameter bar with a 50.0 mm gauge length gives a load of 29.8 kN at the 0.2 percent offset yield point, a maximum load of 41.5 kN, and a final gauge length of 60.4 mm after fracture. Determine the yield strength, the ultimate tensile strength and the percentage elongation, stating which of these describes ductility.
markingGuide: Elongation (and reduction in area) measure ductility; yield strength and UTS are strengths (1 mark)
States that these are engineering values based on the original area (1 mark)
questions.explanation: Dividing each load by the original area $A_0=78.54$ mm$^2$ gives $\sigma_y=379$ MPa and UTS $=528$ MPa. The elongation is $(60.4-50.0)/50.0=20.8$ percent, which is a ductility measure.
